newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China boss in HK stops blaming Patten for trouble.
newsitem.headline: China boss in HK stops blaming Patten for trouble.

text.p: China's top official in Hong Kong lifted his traditional finger of blame away from Governor Chris Patten on Monday and said it was British national policy that had caused Sino-British quarrels over the territory.
The shift of blame came from Zhou Nan, director of the Xinhua News Agency, China's de facto diplomatic mission in Hong Kong, in remarks to the pro-China Wen Wei Po newspaper.

Zhou's remarks, shortly before Britain's Conservative Party was swept out of power by a crushing Labour election victory, contrasted with his and other senior Chinese officials' strong barbs against Patten in the past over how he ran Hong Kong.
Britain's Hong Kong policy has long been viewed as a bipartisan policy, and no major changes are expected by Labour.

Zhou said changes in British policy, in which Patten was only one element, caused the Sino-British squabbles, which have centred on democratic reforms launched under Patten, and China's plans to dismantle them and curb democracy and civil rights.
Britain hands Hong Kong back to China at midnight on June 30, just 60 days away, ending 156 years of colonial rule.
Zhou was quoted as saying Britain underestimated China in the 1990s, thinking the Chinese government would collapse and doubting it would last until the 1997 Hong Kong handover.

He said London had intended to change or overturn the Sino-British accords on the handover, and to turn Hong Kong into a territory led by legislature instead of by an executive, which would have clashed with the agreed post-1997 constitution.
London sought to control the legislature before and after 1997 through the new election system, Wen Wei Po said.
The reforms introduced by Patten returned the territory's first fully-elected legislature in 1995, against China's will.
Zhou also alleged Britain wanted to convert Hong Kong into an independent or semi-independent territory and had changed the law to cut the executive power of the post-colonial government.
